profile.reading:
Data Foundry is a privately held Texas colocation operator. This facility, branded Houston 2 on the operator's own site, sits at 660 Greens Parkway, Houston, Texas 77067, near George Bush Intercontinental Airport in Harris County, and is the only Houston facility named on Data Foundry's current data centers index page. The operator describes Houston 2 as a purpose built, 350,000 square foot building on an 18 acre campus, marketed specifically toward high performance computing workloads, with dual underground utility feeds, 2.25 megawatt Cummins diesel backup generators, and a choice of N+1 to 2N power redundancy depending on customer tier. Data Foundry's own materials cite 60 megawatts of power capacity available to the site, a figure this registry treats as utility service capacity rather than a certified critical IT load rating, so it is not recorded here as a building level IT capacity number.

Data Foundry has operated in Texas for more than two decades, with its current portfolio concentrated in Austin, where it runs three separate facilities tracked elsewhere in this registry as Data Foundry 00 (also called Austin 1), Data Foundry 01, and Data Foundry 02, and this single Houston building. Unlike larger REIT owned or private equity backed operators also tracked in this registry, Data Foundry remains an independent Texas company that does not file SEC disclosures, so this entry's power and redundancy details are sourced solely to the operator's own published materials rather than independent audits or regulatory filings. No year opened date or independently verified megawatt figure was located for this facility in the sourcing reviewed this session.

The Greens Point and North Houston submarket where Houston 2 sits, near the airport rather than Houston's energy corridor core, has become a secondary hub for enterprise and disaster recovery colocation demand, drawing customers who want geographic diversification from the state's larger Dallas and Austin data center clusters. Data Foundry markets its Houston presence specifically toward disaster recovery and business continuity customers headquartered elsewhere in Texas, citing physical distance from its Austin buildings as a selling point for exactly that kind of intra state redundancy planning, a strategy consistent with the company's broader decision to keep its Austin buildings themselves non adjacent rather than consolidated onto one campus.

reading.body:
Data Foundry's Houston facility holds 60 MW of colocation capacity on a 350,000 square foot campus, but the operator does not publicly disclose how much is currently committed to AI workloads.

The facility sits near George Bush Intercontinental Airport in Harris County with dual underground utility feeds and 2.25 MW of backup generation offering N+1 to 2N redundancy. This infrastructure pattern reflects colocation operator standards rather than the single-customer, ultra-high-density builds increasingly favored by large AI labs. Data Foundry markets space to multiple customers across sectors, not exclusively to AI.

The 60 MW capacity ceiling matters for AI scaling only if occupied by inference, training, or supporting infrastructure. Colocation operators typically run at partial utilization and mix workloads. Without disclosed critical IT load figures or customer composition data, the facility's actual contribution to AI compute capacity remains opaque. The power is available to Houston's grid. Whether it serves AI, traditional enterprise, or other uses determines its relevance to compute constraints on AI growth.
